html:
The Carnatic Wars were three wars between the British and French trading companies in south India between 1746 and 1763. The British won, and both sides learnt how a few European-trained soldiers could decide the fate of Indian kingdoms.

The first war, from 1746 to 1748, was a spillover of a European war. The French under Dupleix took Madras. When the nawab of the Carnatic sent 10,000 horsemen to get it back, a few hundred French and Indian infantry with quick-firing guns routed them at the Adyar River. Everyone took note.

In the second, from 1749 to 1754, the two companies were at peace at home and fought through Indian princes, each backing its own man for the thrones of Hyderabad and the Carnatic. Robert Clive, a young clerk turned soldier, seized and held the fort of Arcot for fifty days in 1751 and made his name.

The third, from 1756 to 1763, was part of the Seven Years' War. The British beat the French at Wandiwash in 1760 and took Pondicherry in 1761.

France kept only a few ports. The British kept the method: sepoys, Indian soldiers drilled in the European way, and rulers who paid for them. Clive used both at Plassey.
sum: The Carnatic Wars were three wars between the British and French trading companies in south India between 1746 and 1763. The British won, and both sides learnt how a few European-trained soldiers could decide the fate of Indian kingdoms.
